title: Star Route
subtitle: Rio Seco County, New Mexico Territory, 29 June to 18 July 1881

listing.title: Star Route 📯
listing.blurb: New Mexico Territory, summer 1881. The railroad has come, and the old Rio Seco stage line and its mail contract are finished. On the coach's last run the miners' payroll is taken at gunpoint and the messenger shot dead. The town blames a vaquero's boy, and the cattle and land company that wants the old Spanish grant's commons and the county seat is happy to let it. In twelve days the county votes. Find out who is spending the stolen money. Levels 3–7.

synopsis: For thirteen years the Rio Seco Mail & Stage Line has carried the United States mail, the express and anyone with twelve dollars from Albuquerque seventy miles west to Santa Teresita, the old adobe county seat of Rio Seco County, and on to the silver camp of Plata Vieja in the Sierra Prieta. In February 1881 the Rio Grande & Colorado River Railroad reached a water stop eighteen miles north of the plaza, and the Paragon Townsite & Improvement Company, with St. Louis money, laid out a town there and called it Paragon. From 1 July the mail will go by train to Paragon and on by the Company's own buckboard. Santa Teresita will get its letters twice a week from a Company town. The stage line is finished. The Company wants two more things. It has bought the Lucero family's claim that the Merced de Santa Teresita, a Spanish grant of 1768, was a private grant to one man and not a community grant to twenty-four families. If that claim stands, the grant's commons belong to the Company: a hundred and eighty thousand acres of pasture, timber, springs and coal that the vecinos have grazed and cut in common for a hundred and thirteen years. The Company's suit to quiet its title comes before the district court in Albuquerque on Monday 18 July. And on Tuesday 12 July the county votes on moving the county seat from Santa Teresita to Paragon, and elects a probate judge and three commissioners. Whoever holds the courthouse holds the sheriff who will serve the court's orders. On Thursday 30 June, on the coach's last run, the Plata Vieja mines' June payroll, $9,600, is taken at the Puerto de Piedra by four men on the rocks. Lon Brisbane, the express messenger, is shot dead in the first second. The party are aboard. By Friday night the Paragon Citizens' Committee has posted a $1,000 reward for the Santa Teresita bandits. It names Tiburcio Archibeque, seventeen, a vaquero of the commons, whose sombrero was found where the robbers held their horses. The boy did hold the horses. He was hired as a guide and did not know what for. The robbery was planned by Fenton Rusk, the Company's election agent, with the manager's knowledge, and carried out by a Texas gunman named Cade Rendell and three hired men, with the old driver, Jethro Petree, as their inside man. It was never about the money. The stolen payroll is the miners' own wages, and it will be handed back to them on election day at the Company store in Paragon as an advance on their wages. Each envelope will hold a Progress ticket, and each man will vote in a precinct where he has no right to vote. The rest buys repeaters and two-dollar votes, and the blame falls on the plaza. Over four scenarios, the robbed coach, the grant, the election and the last run, the party can follow the money, find the boy before the Committee does, keep the commons from being fenced, turn the miners at the polls with the bank's own serial numbers, and drive the old coach one last time, seventy miles and a river in flood, to get the witnesses and the grant's papers to Albuquerque before the court opens. Or they can take the reward.
hook: Wednesday 29 June 1881, six in the morning, outside the Southwestern Express office in Albuquerque. Coach No. 7 of the Rio Seco Mail & Stage Line, a mud-red Concord the drivers call la Doña, stands in the street with six fresh horses. On the box sits Jethro Petree, who has driven this road since 1868 and is driving it for the last time. Beside him Lon Brisbane, the express messenger, checks his shotgun. Under their feet, chained to the floor of the boot, is an iron-bound box holding the Plata Vieja mines' June payroll: nine thousand six hundred dollars. The line's owner, Cyprian Ludlow, white-bearded and sixty-six, has come down to see the coach off. He shakes every passenger's hand and tells each one that the line has never lost a mail sack. On the office door a printed notice from the Post Office Department says that from Friday 1 July the mails for Plata Vieja will go by the Rio Grande & Colorado River Railroad to Paragon, and on by the Paragon & Plata Vieja Buckboard Line. Somebody has chalked one word under it in Spanish: ¿Y nosotros? (And us?) Two days and seventy miles to Santa Teresita, a night at the Puerco crossing, then up through the Puerto de Piedra. Old Jethro says it is the prettiest road in the territory, and he would know. You have your seats.

setting.name: Rio Seco County, New Mexico Territory: Santa Teresita, Paragon, Plata Vieja and the Albuquerque road, 29 June to 18 July 1881
setting.description: Rio Seco County, Santa Teresita, Paragon, Plata Vieja and every company in the campaign are fictional; the territory, the year and the history are real. New Mexico has been American since 1846, and a territory since 1850. Its Hispano people became citizens under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848, and in 1881 they are most of its voters, most of its legislature and most of its sheriffs. They are also defending land grants made by Spain and Mexico, some of them two centuries old, before a Surveyor General in Santa Fe who has hundreds of claims and no money, and a Congress that confirms a few each decade. The railroads arrived in 1879 and 1880. Albuquerque has a new town of brick and lumber growing up around the depot, a mile and a half from the old adobe plaza. Every week a new boomtown is platted beside a water tank, and every week another stage line, freighter and plaza is left a day's ride from the future. The county lies west of the Rio Grande, between the Rio Puerco and the Sierra Prieta. Santa Teresita, the county seat, is a plaza town of nine hundred people on the Rio Seco. It has an adobe church, a courthouse that was once the Lucero storehouse, irrigated fields and orchards along the acequia madre, and sheep and cattle on the commons that run south to the mountains. It sits on the Merced de Santa Teresita, granted in 1768 by the Spanish governor at Santa Fe to Ventura Lucero and the twenty-four families who came with him. Each family received house lots and fields. The pastures, waters and woods were left in common, for all. Eighteen miles north, Paragon, the Company's railroad town, is five months old. It has four hundred people, a depot and telegraph, the Paragon House hotel, the Silver Rail Saloon, the Paragon Mercantile, a lumber yard and a brass band, and plans for a courthouse. Twenty-six miles south-west in the Sierra Prieta is Plata Vieja, a silver camp of eleven hundred: Mexican, Hispano, Irish, Welsh, German and Black miners, the Plata Vieja Consolidated's mill, and a new branch of the Paragon Mercantile. North-west, the grant's commons meet the lands of Laguna Pueblo, a nation older than any grant, with its own government, its own lawyers and its own agreement with the railroad. Its men work the section gangs on the new line. The county's people are as mixed as the territory: Hispano farmers, herders and vaqueros who have been here for a hundred years, a rico family that owns half the sheep, Anglo railroaders and boomers, a Welsh widow who teaches the miners' children, a Bavarian Jewish doctor, a Black express messenger from Kansas, Texas gunmen and Laguna section hands. They are neighbours, rivals, customers and voters, and on 12 July most of the men among them will vote.
setting.atmosphere: High, dry, enormous country in the hottest weeks of the year, until the rains come. The llano is pale grass and chamisa under a white sky, the mesas are black basalt and red sandstone, and the Sierra Prieta is a dark line of piñon and juniper in the south. Every afternoon from about 10 July the clouds pile up over the mountains, and by four o'clock there is thunder, a smell of wet dust, and twenty minutes of rain that fills every arroyo with a brown wall of water. Santa Teresita is cool adobe and shade: cottonwoods along the acequia, the church bell, women plastering walls, goats, chile drying on the vigas, a fiddle and guitar at a baile on Saturday night. Paragon is raw lumber, new paint, flies, a brass band practising, locomotive smoke and the clink of the Silver Rail's piano. The coach is dust, heat, leather, horse sweat, the creak of the thoroughbraces and the driver's horn at the stations. The tone is a western paperback with a political novel inside it: a robbery, a manhunt, an election in which money and guns are both on the ballot. The GM should let people argue in Spanish and English, sometimes in the same sentence, and should play the Hispano characters, the Company men and the Laguna foreman as people who believe their own reasons. The Company is not a pack of devils. Some of its people truly think they are bringing the future. The plaza is not a congregation of saints. Its rich man has made a deal, its candidate has taken money, and its precinct boss has bought votes with whiskey for twenty years. What matters is who robbed the coach, who killed Lon Brisbane, and who is going to be made to pay for it.

regions.name: Santa Teresita
regions.description: The county seat and the grant's plaza: a square of adobe houses around a dusty plaza with a cottonwood, the church of Santa Teresa with its two bell towers, and the courthouse, a long low adobe that was the Lucero storehouse until 1852, with the county clerk's office, the records and a two-cell jail. Sheriff Florencio Jaramillo keeps the peace here and is liked for it. The Rio Seco line's home station is on the east side: corrals, a smithy, the station house and Doña Eufemia Ludlow's eating house, where the coach has stopped for thirteen years. Don Fermín Lucero's big house has its own chapel, sala and a hundred-foot portal. Venancio Chávez's cantina, La Golondrina, has a monte bank in the back room. Celestino Trujillo keeps the plaza school. Below the plaza the acequia madre runs along the fields, orchards and chile patches, every family's strip running down to the river. Los Ranchitos, the upper village, is three miles up the river.

regions.name: Paragon
regions.description: The Company's town, eighteen miles north on the railroad: two hundred lots sold and a thousand staked, a main street called Coldiron Avenue, the depot with its water tank and telegraph, the Paragon House hotel, the Silver Rail Saloon, the Paragon Mercantile (the Company store, which sells everything and holds paper on half the county), the Paragon Livery & Feed, a lumber yard, a newspaper called the Paragon Pioneer, and a vacant block with a painted board: SITE OF THE RIO SECO COUNTY COURTHOUSE. Everard Coldiron, the Company's manager, has an office upstairs over the Mercantile. Fenton Rusk, its election agent, has a room at the Paragon House and a table at the Silver Rail. Constable Ott Ebner, appointed by the Company, keeps Paragon's peace. Victoriano Romero's section gang from Laguna works the track east and west of the town.

regions.name: The Commons and the Sierra Prieta
regions.description: The grant's ejido, a hundred and eighty thousand acres of llano, mesa and mountain south and west of the plaza, grazed in common by the vecinos' sheep, goats and cattle under rules a hundred years old. The Ojo del Gato is a cluster of springs fourteen miles south-west, with sheep camps, stone corrals and the Rio Seco line's station on the Plata Vieja road. Since 5 July the Company's surveyor and fence crew have been at work there. The Cañoncito is a box canyon in the foothills with an abandoned sheep camp, eight miles south of the Puerto de Piedra, where Cade Rendell's men lie up after the robbery. The Cerro Colorado is a red hill at the grant's north-west corner, where an old stone cairn marks the boundary between the commons and the pasture of Laguna Pueblo. Someone has moved it. Plata Vieja is in the Sierra Prieta, twenty-six miles south-west of the plaza: one crooked street up a canyon, the Consolidated's ten-stamp mill, saloons, a chapel and the miners' school.

regions.name: The Albuquerque Road
regions.description: The stage road east to Albuquerque, seventy miles. It runs nine miles to the Puerto de Piedra, a gap in a basalt ridge where the road climbs through boulders and the robbery happens. Then twenty miles to La Mesita station, still Ludlow's, and forty to the Puerco station at the Rio Puerco crossing, a wide sandy riverbed that is dry for most of the year and a torrent for an hour after a storm. Ludlow sells that station to the Company on 8 July. Fifty-eight miles out the road climbs the Ceja, the escarpment above the Rio Grande valley. Then it drops through Atrisco to the river and the bridge into Albuquerque's Old Town, with its plaza, the church of San Felipe de Neri and the county courthouse, where the district court sits from Monday 18 July. New Town, around the depot, is a mile and a half east.

campaignRules.name: The Election Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a calendar from Wednesday 29 June to Monday 18 July 1881. Every faction acts on it whether or not the players are watching. st-scenario-001 is the last run and the robbery (29 June to 3 July). st-scenario-002 is the grant (4 to 8 July). st-scenario-003 is the election (9 to 12 July). st-scenario-004 is the last run to Albuquerque (15 to 18 July). Track the date openly. If the players do not interfere, this happens. THE COMPANY: on Thursday 30 June at about 3:40 p.m. Rendell's men rob coach No. 7 at the Puerto de Piedra and kill Lon Brisbane. On Friday 1 July the Company's buckboard carries the first mail and the Paragon Citizens' Committee posts $1,000 for 'the Santa Teresita bandits', naming Tiburcio Archibeque. On Saturday 2 July Constable Ebner and twelve Paragon men ride to the plaza to arrest the boy, and Sheriff Jaramillo refuses to give up his county seat's jail to them. That evening the wire at Paragon brings news that the President has been shot in Washington. On Monday 4 July the Company holds a Fourth of July barbecue for the Progress ticket at Paragon, with free beer paid for in stolen notes. On Tuesday 5 July its handbills at Plata Vieja promise an advance on the miners' June wages, payable at the Paragon Mercantile on election day only. The same day its surveyor and fence crew begin fencing the Ojo del Gato springs, guarded by Rendell's men. On Friday 8 July the Company buys the Puerco station from Ludlow. On Saturday 9 July forty repeaters arrive from Albuquerque on the train. On Monday 11 July the Company's wagons go up to Plata Vieja. On Tuesday 12 July the miners are carried to Paragon, paid and voted there. Before the canvass on Friday 15 July Rusk orders Rendell to kill Jethro Petree and Tiburcio, the two witnesses who can hang him. THE PLAZA: Lon Brisbane's inquest is on Friday 1 July and his funeral on Sunday 3 July. The grant's junta meets in Don Fermín's sala on Wednesday 6 July. The People's ticket rallies on the plaza on Saturday 9 July. On election night the plaza count is run by Venancio Chávez, who owes the Company $600. JETHRO PETREE: he drinks, sleeps badly and tries twice to give back his $100. Unless he is protected, Rendell shoots him on the night of Sunday 10 July. TIBURCIO: he hides at Rufina Sedillo's sheep camp near the Ojo del Gato. If nobody finds him first, the Committee's riders take him on Thursday 7 July and the Paragon crowd means to hang him from the water tank on election night. THE COURT: the district court opens at Albuquerque at ten o'clock on Monday 18 July. The federal grand jury is sworn that morning. The Company's suit to quiet its title to the commons is on the docket, and if no answer is filed that day it goes by default. Whatever the players change, the people they have not touched carry on, adapting only to what they could plausibly know.

campaignRules.name: Two Towns' Reputation
campaignRules.description: Use frontier.json's Reputation rules with two scores, tracked openly and announced when they change: Santa Teresita (the plaza, Los Ranchitos and the commons) and Paragon. Both start at 0. In both towns Reputation rises for fair dealing in public, protecting someone who cannot protect themselves, keeping your word, and walking away clean from a showdown. It falls for bullying, cheating, shooting an unarmed or surrendering man, breaking your word, and standing by at a hanging. The two towns also want different things. In the plaza, Reputation rises for respecting the grant's ways (asking the mayordomo before watering at the acequia, speaking at the junta only when invited, learning a few words of Spanish) and falls for treating the vecinos as foreigners in their own county. In Paragon it rises for being useful to business and falls for siding with the plaza in public. The GM also tracks three attitudes as hostile, wary, neutral, friendly or trusting: the Company's, the People's party's, and the miners'. They move with what the party does for or against each. The miners start wary of everyone, because nobody has paid them. At Santa Teresita +3, the sheriff deputizes the party and the vecinos hide whoever they ask. At Paragon +3, the depot telegrapher will let a friend look at the book. At -3 in either town nobody sells you cartridges or feed. At -5 in Paragon, the Committee comes for you.

campaignRules.name: Follow the Money
campaignRules.description: The mystery inside the election runs on the three-clue rule. Every conclusion the players need has at least three clues in different places, named in the control file (lettered A to F) and in each scenario. Core clues are found by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill, without a roll. Rolls add detail, speed or safety, and a failed roll costs time, a horse, Reputation or a faction's goodwill, never the truth. The spine of the case is paper money. Of the payroll, $6,000 was new $10 and $5 national bank notes of the Bank of the Rio Abajo. The bank's cashier wrote their serial numbers on a schedule pinned to the express waybill: tens B 4401 to B 4700, fives A 2201 to A 2800. Tabitha Lockhart carries the messenger's copy; the bank and the Southwestern Express office in Albuquerque have the others. Any note in those ranges is stolen. From 4 July they turn up in Paragon: in the Silver Rail's till, in repeaters' pockets, in two-dollar votes, and in the miners' 'advance on wages' envelopes. If the party wires Albuquerque for the schedule from the Paragon depot, Rusk reads the wire within the hour and starts changing notes at the Mercantile's safe for old ones. That slows the trail but does not end it. If the table is stuck, have a companion lay the case out by lamplight: who knew which coach carried the money, whose horses wore factory shoes, who ordered pay envelopes ten days before there was any reason to, and whose store is paying the miners.

campaignRules.name: The Vote
campaignRules.description: The election on Tuesday 12 July is a contest the party can see, count and change. Voting is by printed ticket, handed in at the polls in front of the judges. There is no secret ballot in 1881, and everyone knows how everyone votes. A voter must be a male citizen of twenty-one who has lived in the county six months. Removal of the county seat needs a majority of the votes cast. The honest count, if nobody cheats, is People's 605 and Progress 415: Santa Teresita 260 to 170 (Don Fermín's 120 partidarios voting Progress), Los Ranchitos 120 to 30, Paragon 20 to 120, Plata Vieja 150 to 90 among its 240 citizen miners, and the Ojo del Gato sheep camps 55 to 5. The Company's plan, and what each part is worth to its margin: (1) carry the Plata Vieja miners to Paragon, pay them their own stolen wages, and vote all of them there, the 240 citizens and 140 Mexican nationals who have no vote anywhere, worth about 420; (2) vote 120 railroad men in Paragon who arrived in February and are four months short of residence, worth 120; (3) forty repeaters from Albuquerque who vote in Paragon and again at Los Ranchitos, worth 60; (4) two-dollar votes on the plaza, about 40 votes moved, worth 80; (5) a crooked count on the plaza, if Venancio Chávez does what the Company's note on his debts asks, 60 votes moved, worth 120. If all five work, Progress wins by about 600. Each can be stopped. Show the miners the serial numbers and most of them refuse the envelopes and go home to vote: that takes back the 420. Put sworn challengers with the county's residence list at the Paragon poll: 120. Spot the repeaters, whom Theodora Quayle or Venancio will know: 60. Watch the plaza: 80. Keep Venancio honest: 120. Turn Don Fermín and his 120 partidarios vote People's (240) or stay home (120). Keep a running tally in world state and tell the players what each thing they do is worth, in votes. The result matters, but it is not the end: a stolen election can be contested in the district court by Monday 18 July, if the evidence gets there.

campaignRules.name: The Grant
campaignRules.description: What the GM needs to know about the grant, said plainly. The Merced de Santa Teresita was a community grant. In 1768 the governor gave Ventura Lucero and twenty-four families house lots and irrigated fields to own, and pastures, waters and woods to use in common forever. The proof is the act of possession: the alcalde's record of walking the boundaries and naming the families. The petition alone names only Lucero. Under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo the United States promised to respect such grants. In practice they wait years for the Surveyor General's report and Congress's confirmation, and meanwhile anyone who buys a few heirs' rights can sue. The Company's private-grant claim rests on the petition and on deeds from Don Fermín Lucero and three cousins. The community's answer rests on the act of possession, on a hundred years of common use, and on witnesses. The irrigated fields and the acequia are run by the vecinos, who each spring elect a mayordomo to share out the water by turns, so that everyone downstream gets some. The commons are grazed under the grant's own rules. Laguna Pueblo's lands lie to the north-west, under its own Spanish grant. Its boundary with the commons is marked by stone cairns that both communities walked in 1856, and the pueblo has its own governor, council and lawyer. Its man in this story, Victoriano Romero, speaks for Laguna's interest, which is its own boundary, and not for either side of the county's election. Play every grant character as a person with their own politics: herders who need the commons, a rico who thinks a deal is the only way to save anything, a schoolmaster who wants both the commons and the railroad, women who hold water rights and speak at the acequia meeting. Never play them as a backdrop.

campaignRules.name: Coach and Road
campaignRules.description: Use combat.json's vehicles and chases and frontier.json's horses, trail travel and weather. Coach No. 7, la Doña, is a Concord (AC 12, HP 60, 10 mph on the road, six horses, nine inside, three on the roof). The express box, AC 15, HP 20, Mechanics DC 15 to open, rides chained in the front boot under the driver's seat. Teams are changed every ten to fifteen miles. A team that is not changed covers its next ten miles at half speed and the coach has disadvantage in chases. Stations east from Santa Teresita: Puerto de Piedra 9 miles (no station), La Mesita 20, Puerco 40 (the Company's from 8 July, and it will not sell you a horse), the Ceja 58, Atrisco 66, Old Town Albuquerque 70. North to Paragon is 18 miles, about three hours. South-west to the Ojo del Gato is 14, and on to Plata Vieja another 12. From 10 July the afternoon storms fill the arroyos. A flash flood in the Rio Puerco runs for 1d4 hours and cannot be forded while it runs. Driving a coach in a chase uses Animal Handling, and the person on the box with the lines is the only one who can make the check. A good horse is part of a character: name it. Showdowns use frontier.json. Cade Rendell will fight a showdown when he has an audience and the sun behind him, and in no other way. A fair fight in the street raises Reputation in that town; a shot from cover lowers it by 2.

explorationRules: This is a county sandbox with a road through it, and the map is a schematic: Paragon and the railroad in the north, the plaza in the middle on the Rio Seco, the commons and the Sierra Prieta to the south and west with Plata Vieja in the mountains, Laguna's boundary at the Cerro Colorado, and the Albuquerque road running east through the Puerto de Piedra to the Puerco crossing and the city. The party moves on horseback, by buckboard, by the Company's train from Paragon (if they dare) or, at the end, on the old coach. The unit of time is the half-day. The Election Clock (campaignRules) is the engine: every half-day spent somewhere is a half-day not spent somewhere else, and the factions keep moving. In session one the party is aboard the coach, and after the robbery they choose who they work for: the Southwestern Express Company's reward ($500 for the box, $250 a head for the robbers), Cyprian Ludlow's honour, the mine's payroll, the sheriff's deputy badges, the plaza and the boy, or the Committee's $1,000 for Tiburcio Archibeque. Each pregen's sheet suggests one. Run each scenario as a set of named places, with each faction acting on its schedule and on what it could know. Nobody is omniscient. Rusk knows what Rendell, the depot telegrapher and the Mercantile's clerks tell him. The plaza knows what its vecinos see. Don Fermín knows only what Coldiron has chosen to show him. The mystery follows the three-clue rule. Fights are short, loud and consequential, and most scenes are a conversation across a portal, a monte table, a ledger or a ballot box with someone who wants something. Between scenes let the country breathe: a roadrunner on the coach road, a burro under a load of piñon wood, a church bell at noon, a locomotive's whistle across twenty miles of llano, thunderheads building over the Sierra Prieta. Money is 1881 dollars. A miner earns $3 a day, a vaquero $25 a month and found, stage fare to Albuquerque is $12, a good horse costs $60, a vote costs $2, and the commons are worth more than anyone in the county can count. The players should come away knowing what Rio Seco County looked like the summer the railroad came, and feeling that whatever they chose, it cost someone something.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Rio Seco County, Santa Teresita, Paragon, Plata Vieja, the Merced de Santa Teresita, the Rio Seco Mail & Stage Line, the Paragon Townsite & Improvement Company, the Rio Grande & Colorado River Railroad, the Southwestern Express Company, the Bank of the Rio Abajo and every person in the campaign are fictional. Some things are real history: New Mexico Territory in 1881, the arrival of the railroads and the death of the stage lines, star-route mail contracts, Spanish and Mexican land grants and their commons, the Surveyor General's office, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, county-seat fights, vote-buying and repeaters in territorial elections, the shooting of the President on 2 July 1881, Albuquerque's Old Town and New Town, and Laguna Pueblo, whose men did work on the railroad's section gangs under an agreement with the line. This is an analogue of those things, not a retelling of any one event, and no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: The Paragon Townsite & Improvement Company was formed in St. Louis in 1880 to own the town at the railroad's water stop. Its manager is Everard Coldiron, 44, a former railroad land agent. The townsite stands on the north edge of the Santa Teresita commons, so the Company needs the commons to be private land with a title it can hold. In March 1881 it bought the Lucero private-grant claim from Don Fermín Lucero, the founder's great-grandson and the richest man in the county, and from three cousins, for $15,000 and stock. Don Fermín was promised in writing that the vecinos' house lots, fields and water would be excepted. They are not excepted. The Company's plat of a 'Paragon South Addition and Rio Seco Irrigation District' lays lots and a reservoir over the plaza's fields and the acequia's headgate, and its quiet-title suit, filed in May, asks the court to remove 'all occupants and trespassers' from the whole grant. Don Fermín has not seen either. The Company also got the Paragon–Plata Vieja mail contract through a subsidiary, killing the Rio Seco line, and it got the legislature to call a county-seat election for 12 July. Its election agent is Fenton Rusk, 50, a Santa Fe political fixer. Rusk did the arithmetic in June: the honest vote loses by nearly two hundred, and the Plata Vieja miners are the difference. They hate the Company store, and they vote People's. Rusk's answer was to take their June payroll, $9,600, which comes from Albuquerque on the last stage of every month, and to give it back to them himself. On 20 June he ordered four hundred pay envelopes printed in Albuquerque, PARAGON MERCANTILE — ADVANCE ON WAGES, ten days before the payroll was stolen. He told Coldiron in plain words what he meant to do. Coldiron answered that he did not want to know how, and wrote to St. Louis that 'the miners' payroll difficulty will be settled to our advantage before the 12th'. Rusk hired Cade Rendell, 38, a Texas gunman, with Shad Sorrel, Lige Tasker and Hob Linnet, at $500 each plus the payroll's $3,600 in coin. They stayed at the Paragon House from 22 to 27 June on the Company's account and hired four horses from the Paragon Livery, shod with factory shoes. On 24 June Rusk met Jethro Petree, 61, the line's oldest driver, in Paragon. He offered Petree the head driver's job on the new buckboard line at $90 a month, and $500 in gold, $100 down, to tell Rendell where the box rode and to halt the coach at the top of the Puerto de Piedra grade when he saw a red rag on a juniper. Rusk swore nobody would be hurt. On 27 June Lige Tasker hired Tiburcio Archibeque, 17, at the Ojo del Gato for $20, to guide 'four horse buyers' over the old sheep trail. Tiburcio held their horses in the arroyo below the gap. Shad Sorrel, raised in San Antonio, gave the orders at the coach in Spanish, so the passengers would remember Spanish. On Thursday 30 June at 3:40 p.m. Petree halted at the rag. Rendell shot Lon Brisbane, the messenger, through the chest from 200 yards with a .50 buffalo rifle. He had decided days before that an armed messenger was a risk, and he had not told Rusk. Sorrel and Tasker covered the coach from the rocks while Rendell and Linnet came up out of the arroyo and took the box. Tiburcio heard the shot, saw the dead man and ran. He lost his sombrero, with T.A. burned inside the band, and Rendell picked it up and dropped it where it would be found. At the Cañoncito the gang broke the box. They kept the coin and sent the $6,000 in notes to Rusk by Hob Linnet, who left at dawn on 1 July by the sheep trail and reached Paragon that night. Rusk is spending them: free beer at the Fourth of July barbecue, $5 a day for forty repeaters, $2 votes, and $4,560 in envelopes of $12 a man for the miners, to be handed out at the Mercantile in Paragon on election day with a Progress ticket inside. The miners will vote in Paragon, where they have no right to vote, with their own wages in their pockets. The robbery also lets the Company blame the plaza, through Tiburcio and the Spanish, and puts the People's candidate's own nephew on a reward poster a week before the vote. Nobody but the bank's cashier, the express company and Tabitha Lockhart knows that the notes' serial numbers were written down. Rusk does not. Petree did not know anyone would die. He is coming apart, and Rusk has told Rendell to finish him and the boy before the court sits.
suspects: Fenton Rusk, 50, the Company's election agent, Paragon House and the Silver Rail: the man who planned the robbery. Motive: the election. Plan: hand the miners their stolen wages in Paragon, vote them there, buy the rest, blame the plaza, then silence Petree and Tiburcio before the court sits on 18 July. THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Everard Coldiron, 44, manager of the Paragon Townsite & Improvement Company: he approved the plan without hearing it and wrote to St. Louis about it. He wants the county seat, the commons and the plaza's water, and he believes Paragon is the future. He will sacrifice Rusk the moment Rusk becomes a risk.

Cade Rendell, 38, a Texas gunman: the man who shot Lon Brisbane from 200 yards with a .50 buffalo rifle. Fast, vain and careful. He wants his money, and he wants a famous showdown before he leaves the territory. Rusk has given him Petree and the boy to kill.

Jethro Petree, 61, the line's oldest driver: the inside man. He halted the coach at the red rag for $100 in gold and a job. He did not know anyone would be shot, and Lon Brisbane was his friend. He will confess to someone he trusts if he lives long enough.

Tiburcio Archibeque, 17, a vaquero of the commons: the boy on the poster. He held the robbers' horses for $20, not knowing what for, and ran when he heard the shot. He is hiding at Rufina Sedillo's sheep camp, and he is the only witness who saw all four robbers' faces.

Don Fermín Lucero, 61, the Company's candidate for probate judge: he sold the Lucero claim on the promise that the fields and water would be spared. He is innocent of the robbery and will be horrified by it, and he does not know what the Company means to do with the plaza's water.
redHerrings: Tiburcio Archibeque and the plaza's young men. The sombrero, the Spanish at the coach, and a vaquero's unshod cow pony in the tracks all point at the plaza. Tiburcio did hold the horses. He is a frightened boy who was hired as a guide, and once he trusts the party he is the best witness in the county.

Cyprian Ludlow robbed his own coach out of spite or for money. The Paragon Pioneer hints at it on Saturday 2 July. Ludlow is broke and bitter, but the express company carries the loss, not the line. The robbery ruins what is left of his name, and he would rather die than lose a mail sack.

Hamish Gow, superintendent of the Plata Vieja Consolidated, arranged the robbery to hide a failing mine. The mine's credit is tight and he was slow with the May wages. He is innocent of the robbery. He has a smaller secret: on 15 June he gave Celestino Trujillo $300 for the People's ticket, because a Company county seat would tax his road and his ore. The Company would love to print that.

Lon Brisbane was in on it. He had faro debts at the Silver Rail, and the Committee says the messenger 'opened the box for his friends'. Lon was shot first because he was the one man on the coach who would have fought. His debts were paid off by Tabitha Lockhart, his partner, in May.
clues: A. THE ROBBERS WERE NOT SANTA TERESITA MEN. A1: the tracks in the arroyo: four horses in factory-made shoes of the kind the Paragon Livery buys by the keg, and one unshod cow pony; the plaza's smiths forge their own (st-scenario-001). A2: the robber who spoke Spanish at the coach used Texas border words and could not roll his r's, and the leader called the orders in English with a Texas drawl (st-scenario-001). A3: at the riflemen's position, .44 cartridge cases and an empty cartridge box with the Paragon Mercantile's price stamp (st-scenario-001). A4: Lon Brisbane was killed by a .50 buffalo-rifle ball from about 200 yards; no vecino owns such a rifle, and Rendell's is the only one in the county (st-scenario-001). A5: Tiburcio's own account, once he is found and trusts the party (st-scenario-001 or 002).

B. CADE RENDELL'S MEN DID IT. B1: the Paragon House register: 'C. Rendell and three, 22 to 27 June', charged to the Company's account on Rusk's signature (st-scenario-001 or 003). B2: the Paragon Livery's book: four horses hired on 27 June by 'L. Tasker', one returned lame on 1 July (st-scenario-001 or 003). B3: Tiburcio was hired by Lige Tasker at the Ojo del Gato on 27 June, and the old herder at the springs saw it (st-scenario-002). B4: Victoriano Romero, whose section house is beside the Paragon Livery, saw the four ride out south at dawn on 27 June with Lige Tasker leading, and saw one of them, Hob Linnet, ride back in on a lame horse with heavy saddlebags on the night of 1 July (st-scenario-001 or 002). B5: the broken express box and the cartridge cases at the Cañoncito camp (st-scenario-001 or 002). B6: the confession of Jethro Petree, Hob Linnet or any gang member taken alive (st-scenario-002 to 004).

C. THE COMPANY PAID FOR IT. C1: the serial-number schedule on the waybill, tens B 4401 to B 4700 and fives A 2201 to A 2800 (st-scenario-001). C2: stolen notes surface in Paragon after 4 July: the Silver Rail's till, repeaters' pockets, two-dollar votes, and the miners' envelopes (st-scenario-002 and 003). C3: the Albuquerque printer's order for four hundred PARAGON MERCANTILE — ADVANCE ON WAGES envelopes, dated 20 June and signed by Rusk; Theodora Quayle remembers the telegram that confirmed it, and the printer's bill is in the Mercantile's files (st-scenario-002 or 003). C4: Jethro Petree's $100 in new double eagles, paid in Paragon on 24 June; his wife spends one at the plaza store on 2 July (st-scenario-001 or 002). C5: Coldiron's letterpress copybook: 'the miners' payroll difficulty will be settled to our advantage before the 12th', written 21 June (st-scenario-003). C6: Petree's, Linnet's or Rendell's word that Rusk paid them (st-scenario-002 to 004).

D. THE COMPANY MEANS TO BUY THE ELECTION. D1: the handbill at Plata Vieja on 5 July: an advance on June wages, payable at the Paragon Mercantile, 12 July only (st-scenario-002). D2: the Paragon poll list: 260 names, 120 of them railroad men who arrived in February, and twenty at lot numbers that are still sagebrush (st-scenario-003). D3: the Company's wagons booked to carry the miners down on 11 and 12 July (st-scenario-003). D4: the forty repeaters off the Saturday train, paid $5 a day in stolen notes (st-scenario-003). D5: the Progress tickets printed on the same yellow card and in the same type as the People's, with SANTA TERESITA across the top and the Company's names underneath (st-scenario-003).

E. THE COMMONS ARE THE PRIZE, AND DON FERMÍN HAS BEEN DECEIVED. E1: Don Fermín's deed of March 1881, with its written exception for 'the house lots, fields and waters of the vecinos' (st-scenario-002). E2: the Company's plat of the Paragon South Addition, with lots and a reservoir over the plaza's fields and the acequia's headgate, in the surveyor's tent at the Ojo del Gato or in Coldiron's office (st-scenario-002 or 003). E3: the quiet-title petition, asking that 'all occupants and trespassers' be removed from the whole grant (st-scenario-002). E4: the Cerro Colorado cairn, moved a mile and a half west by the Company's surveyor, Ozias Hornaday, to put Paragon's new wells inside the 'Lucero grant'; Victoriano Romero and Rufina Sedillo can both show where it stood (st-scenario-002). E5: the original act of possession of 1768, naming the twenty-four families and the commons 'for all', hidden by Rufina's late husband in the wall of her house (st-scenario-002).

F. JETHRO PETREE IS THE INSIDE MAN, AND HE IS MARKED. F1: Petree halted the team at the top of the grade a hundred yards before the felled juniper, though he could not yet have seen it from the bend; a red rag is tied to a juniper on the ridge (st-scenario-001). F2: his double eagles (C4) (st-scenario-001 or 002). F3: the buckboard line's letter offering him the head driver's job from 1 August, in his coat (st-scenario-002). F4: Rendell in the Silver Rail, overheard or reported, asking where the old man sleeps (st-scenario-003).
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve it when they stop asking who robbed the coach and start asking who is spending the money. Everything turns on the serial numbers. Make sure the party has the schedule by the end of the first scenario, through Tabitha's waybill, the express agent or the bank. Then put a stolen ten-dollar note in front of them in Paragon on the Fourth of July, in the Silver Rail's change or in a repeater's hand. The second hinge is the envelopes. A Company that ordered four hundred 'advance on wages' envelopes ten days before the miners had any wages to advance knew the payroll would not arrive. If the party reaches the election knowing only that the plaza didn't do it, have Thomasina Bevan bring one of the Company's handbills down from Plata Vieja and ask them, in front of the miners, where a store gets $4,560 in cash on a week's notice.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. THE ROBBERY: Rendell and his men can be killed, caught or run out of the territory. Rusk falls only on evidence that reaches a court: the serial numbers matched to notes he paid out, plus the envelope order, plus Petree's or a gang member's confession. Then the federal grand jury indicts him for robbing the mail, and the territory for Lon Brisbane's murder. Coldiron falls only if his copybook letter goes with them, and even then St. Louis's lawyers will get him off with a fine. A party that lets Paragon hang Rendell from the water tank has done what Paragon meant to do to Tiburcio. THE ELECTION: if the party stops enough of the Company's plan, the county seat stays at Santa Teresita and Celestino Trujillo is probate judge. If not, Paragon wins, and the result can still be contested at Albuquerque on 18 July with the evidence. THE GRANT: if the community's answer, the act of possession and its witnesses reach the court on 18 July, the quiet-title suit is stayed until the Surveyor General reports, the fence comes down, and the commons stay common for now. If not, the Company takes a default decree and the sheriff, whoever he is, serves the eviction. DON FERMÍN: if he sees the plat and the petition, he breaks with the Company in public, and that decides most of his partidarios' votes and his own conscience. TIBURCIO AND PETREE: either can die. If the boy dies the plaza never forgives anyone. If Petree dies, Rafael Candelaria grieves a man he can no longer respect. THE LINE: whatever happens, the Rio Seco line does not survive the railroad. If the last run reaches Albuquerque, Cyprian Ludlow sells his horses, keeps la Doña, and the plaza hires him to carry its own mail twice a week on a little branch route of its own. THE EPILOGUE: the GM should end with a line of true history. In 1891 Congress will create the Court of Private Land Claims, and in 1897 the Supreme Court will rule that a community grant's commons belonged to the sovereign, not to the community. Grant after grant will lose its commons to the government, and later to whoever buys them. What the party won in 1881 may be lost in 1897. It was still worth winning, and the vecinos will still be there.
